title: $1,035M EBITDA and the $7.25B acquisition program
body:
## A Year That Reframed the IPP Category

Fiscal year 2025 closed a chapter on what Talen Energy had been — a reorganised Pennsylvania power producer emerging from bankruptcy — and opened an argument about what it might become. Adjusted EBITDA of $1,035 million against adjusted free cash flow of $524 million produced a cash-conversion ratio of precisely 50%, a figure that analysts covering independent power producers treat as a threshold separating capital-intensive generation businesses from genuinely cash-generative ones. For a company that had exited Chapter 11 less than two years earlier, the headline numbers signalled something more than recovery. They signalled structural repositioning.

The $1,035 million figure sits atop a 13.1-gigawatt portfolio that, in its composition, differs substantially from the mid-2010s vintage IPP playbook. The nuclear anchor at Susquehanna, the RMR contracts on the Maryland coast, the record PJM capacity-auction clearance, and the nascent Amazon PPA revenue layer do not move together with gas spot prices in the way that an unhedged gas-weighted fleet would. That layering — contracted, regulated-adjacent, and merchant, weighted toward the first two — is the architectural choice that informed both the $7.25 billion acquisition program and the capital structure assembled to fund it.

## The Susquehanna Economic Engine

The arithmetic of Susquehanna Station is stark. Talen's 90% ownership share of the 2.5-gigawatt facility generated approximately 17 terawatt-hours in fiscal 2025, at an implied levelised cost of electricity of roughly $27 per megawatt-hour. The production cost basis for the year was therefore approximately $459 million — a figure that includes fuel, operations, maintenance, and nuclear decommissioning trust contributions but not the capital cost of the plant, which was written down through the bankruptcy process and now sits on the balance sheet at reorganisation value rather than replacement cost.

That $27 per megawatt-hour cost basis is not an abstraction. It represents one of the most competitive electricity generation cost structures on the PJM interconnection, a grid spanning thirteen Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states that dispatches power in economic merit order. In a market where new gas combined-cycle capacity prices at $50 to $70 per megawatt-hour all-in, and where new solar-plus-storage in the region runs higher still, Susquehanna occupies a position of structural advantage that compounds as carbon constraints tighten.

The Amazon Power Purchase Agreement, initially signed in March 2024 and expanded in June 2025, converts that cost advantage into contracted revenue. The June 2025 expansion brought the agreement to up to 1,920 megawatts of carbon-free baseload power, delivered to an Amazon data center campus adjacent to the Susquehanna site in northeastern Pennsylvania and to other facilities in the state, through 2042 — a tenor of roughly seventeen years from the expansion date. The ramp to full contracted volume extends to approximately 2032, reflecting the physical buildout of the campus and interconnection constraints. Talen has not disclosed the per-megawatt-hour contract price. Industry benchmarks for hyperscaler carbon-free baseload PPAs in the Mid-Atlantic region at the time of execution placed comparable agreements in a range of $80 to $120 per megawatt-hour. Even at the low end of that range, the spread against a $27 per megawatt-hour cost basis implies a material and durable EBITDA contribution that will grow as contracted volumes ramp.

The two companies also announced exploration of co-development of small modular reactors within Talen's Pennsylvania footprint — a long-dated optionality that does not figure in near-term financial projections but signals the depth of the commercial relationship and Amazon's stated preference for co-location with zero-carbon generation rather than renewable-energy-certificate-backed offsite agreements.

## Three Revenue Layers Above the Merchant Base

Independent power producers that depend entirely on energy market clearing prices carry earnings volatility that makes debt markets and equity investors price in a risk premium. Talen's revenue architecture, as it stood at the fiscal year 2025 close, rested on three contracted or quasi-contracted layers stacked above whatever commodity price the residual fleet earns in the spot market.

The first layer is the Reliability Must-Run contracts on Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner, two coal units on the Chesapeake Bay in Maryland that PJM identified as critical for local reliability. The RMR agreements, which took effect in June 2025 and run through May 2029, pay Talen $145 million annually for Brandon Shores and $35 million annually for H.A. Wagner — a combined $180 million per year in fixed revenue regardless of power prices. Across the four remaining years of the contracts at the snapshot date, that represents $720 million of cumulative guaranteed revenue from a grid operator with the balance sheet of the federal government behind it. Management has characterised these plants as candidates for eventual decommissioning or conversion, but through 2029 they function as annuity cash flows.

The second layer is capacity market revenue from PJM's Base Residual Auction. In the 2027/2028 delivery-year auction, Talen cleared 8,745 megawatts at a record clearing price of $333.44 per megawatt-day — a price that reflected tight reserve margins in PJM following years of premature retirements and demand growth driven in part by data center loads in Northern Virginia. At that price and volume, the annualised capacity revenue stream from the 2027/2028 year amounts to approximately $1.06 billion. Capacity payments do not cover fuel or variable operating costs, but they provide revenue certainty well in advance of the delivery period and allow Talen to underwrite fixed costs across the fleet with greater precision than energy-market revenue alone would permit.

The third and structurally most significant layer is the Amazon PPA. Its contribution in fiscal 2025 reflected only the first year of a ramp that will build toward 1,920 megawatts of contracted delivery by approximately 2032. As that volume grows, it will progressively convert Susquehanna's merchant exposure into long-term contracted revenue at prices substantially above current spot power in PJM.

| Revenue Layer | Annual Run Rate | Tenor / Term |
|---|---|---|
| RMR (Brandon Shores + H.A. Wagner) | $180M | Through May 2029 |
| PJM Capacity (2027/28 delivery year) | ~$1,060M | Annual auction cycle |
| Amazon PPA (ramping to 1,920 MW) | Undisclosed; ramp through ~2032 | Through 2042 |

## The Acquisition Program: $7.25 Billion for 5.3 Gigawatts

The fiscal 2025 financial results were assembled on a portfolio that did not yet include the gas capacity acquired and agreed during the year. The $7.25 billion acquisition program represents the most consequential capital allocation decision in Talen's post-reorganisation history, and its logic is inseparable from the PJM capacity market dynamics that produced the $333.44 per megawatt-day clearing price.

The Freedom and Guernsey transaction — two natural gas combined-cycle facilities totalling 2.8 gigawatts — closed during fiscal 2025 at $3.8 billion, implying a transaction price of approximately $1,357 per kilowatt. For context, new-build gas combined-cycle capacity in PJM at comparable heat-rate specifications was being quoted in the $1,800 to $2,200 per kilowatt range during 2025, reflecting supply-chain constraints on turbines and balance-of-plant equipment. Acquiring operating facilities below new-build cost, in a market where new-build lead times stretch to seven years or more, is a form of scarcity arbitrage. Freedom and Guernsey immediately participate in the capacity market, earn energy margin, and require no permitting or interconnection queue risk.

The Cornerstone transaction, agreed but not closed at the snapshot date, adds 2.0 gigawatts of combined-cycle capacity and 456 megawatts of peaking capacity — 2,456 megawatts in total — for $3.45 billion, implying approximately $1,404 per kilowatt across the full package. The marginal premium over Freedom and Guernsey likely reflects competitive tension in the market for premium gas assets as other IPPs pursued similar consolidation strategies.

Taken together, the two transactions add approximately 5.3 gigawatts of gas capacity for $7.25 billion, raising the pro-forma fleet to roughly 18.4 gigawatts. The gas fleet, in the PJM capacity market context, is not merely a merchant earnings stream — it is a portfolio of capacity awards, each of which clears the annual auction and generates revenue before a single megawatt-hour of energy is dispatched.

## Capital Structure and the 3.5x Discipline

Funding a $7.25 billion acquisition program while maintaining investment-grade-adjacent leverage requires debt issuance at scale. Talen executed two senior unsecured notes offerings: $1.4 billion of 6.250% notes due 2034 and $1.3 billion of 6.500% notes due 2036, raising $2.7 billion of long-duration fixed-rate debt in a rate environment that had moved against issuers. The coupon levels — 6.25% and 6.50% — reflect the company's sub-investment-grade credit profile post-reorganisation, but the maturities of 2034 and 2036 provide a runway through which the contracted revenue layers and the gas acquisitions can season before refinancing risk materialises.

The remaining acquisition funding comes from a combination of adjusted free cash flow — $524 million in fiscal 2025 alone — and, where applicable, assumption of existing project-level debt. Management has stated a net leverage target of around 3.5 times or lower over the cycle, a formulation that signals acceptance of peak leverage above that level during the acquisition phase, with a path toward deleveraging as EBITDA grows. At $1,035 million of fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA, $2.7 billion of new notes issuance represents approximately 2.6 turns of incremental debt — manageable if the acquisition program delivers the EBITDA contribution embedded in transaction underwriting.

The 50% FCF-to-EBITDA conversion ratio is the mechanism through which deleveraging occurs without asset sales. At $524 million of adjusted free cash flow in fiscal 2025, the company generates, on an annualised basis, enough cash to retire roughly one-fifth of the new notes issuance in a single year if it directed all free cash toward debt reduction rather than further capital deployment.

## Operating Leverage: The Path to FY27-28

The financial architecture described above creates a specific kind of operating leverage. Susquehanna's cost structure — approximately $459 million in annual production costs — does not scale with revenue. Whether the plant earns merchant pricing in PJM or contracted Amazon PPA pricing, the fuel and operating cost base is essentially fixed. Each incremental dollar of contracted revenue above the cost basis flows nearly unimpaired to EBITDA.

As the Amazon PPA ramps from its current partial-volume delivery toward the 1,920-megawatt contracted ceiling by approximately 2032, and as Freedom, Guernsey, and Cornerstone contribute a full year's capacity revenue for the first time in the 2027/2028 delivery year, the revenue base will be substantially larger than what produced $1,035 million of adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2025. The fixed-cost base of the nuclear and gas operations will not grow commensurately. The result — barring commodity price deterioration or operational setbacks — is a step-change in EBITDA that could move the metric materially higher by fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

That trajectory is the operating-leverage thesis that informed a $7.25 billion capital commitment and $2.7 billion of new debt in a single fiscal year. Talen's management and board — populated with veterans of Texas Competitive Electric Holdings, GenOn, Exelon, and Apollo — have navigated at least one full power-market cycle each. The bet they have made, expressed in capital structure and acquisition terms, is that the AI electricity demand wave sustains long enough for the contracted revenue architecture to compound, and that PJM's supply shortfall persists through the capacity auction cycles that determine whether the gas fleet earns its cost of capital.
